title: Babylon
summary: The imperial city that becomes a biblical symbol of exile, judgment, and arrogant worldly power.
historical_context: Babylon became the Neo-Babylonian imperial capital under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II, received deported Judeans after the campaigns against Jerusalem, and passed to Cyrus in 539 BCE. Judean communities remained in Babylonia through the Persian period.
ancient_near_east_context: Babylon was a large Mesopotamian political, cultic, economic, and scribal center. Royal inscriptions, chronicles, palace ration lists, and private legal documents represent different institutions and social locations; none alone describes the whole city or empire.
hebraic_worldview: Biblical texts portray Babylon as both a concrete place of displaced life and an imperial power accountable to God. Jeremiah calls deportees to long residence and communal welfare, while laments and prophetic texts preserve loss, protest, and hope.
second_temple_context: Persian-period return began from a Babylonian imperial setting but did not end the diaspora. Babylonian Judean documents continuing into the fifth century BCE complicate any picture of universal departure.
canonical_context: Historical Babylon anchors Kings, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Ezra; prophetic and apocalyptic reuse later turns Babylon into a symbol of arrogant or oppressive empire. Historical and symbolic uses should be distinguished.
literary_context: Kings narrates deportation to Babylon, Jeremiah addresses communities there, Ezekiel dates visions from Babylonia, Psalm 137 laments there, and Ezra opens with movement out of Babylon. Revelation's Babylon is later symbolic reuse rather than a direct description of the excavated city.
covenantal_significance: The biblical writers interpret Babylonian conquest as covenant judgment and Persian-period return as mercy; Babylonian texts provide political and social evidence without expressing those covenant claims.
canonical_role: Imperial exile city and recurring biblical symbol of proud human empire, covenant judgment, diaspora testing, and eventual divine overthrow.
